title.en: How LLMs Work: Tokens, Embeddings & Attention
title.ta: LLM-கள் எவ்வாறு வேலை செய்கின்றன: Tokens, Embeddings & Attention

description.en: Understand the inner workings of Large Language Models — tokenization, embeddings, and the attention mechanism explained simply.
description.ta: பெரிய மொழி மாதிரிகளின் உள் செயல்பாடுகளைப் புரிந்துகொள்ளுங்கள் — tokenization, embeddings, attention mechanism எளிமையாக விளக்கப்படுகிறது.

story_variants.en:
## Vaathiyaar's Brain Factory

Vaathiyaar draws a brain on the whiteboard. "Students, an LLM is like a massive prediction engine. Given 'The cat sat on the ___', it predicts 'mat' because it has seen this pattern millions of times. But HOW does it do this? Three steps: Tokenize, Embed, Attend."

### Step 1: Tokenization

Text is split into **tokens** — subword pieces, not full words.

```
'Hello, PyMasters!' → ['Hello', ',', ' Py', 'Masters', '!']
```

- GPT-4: ~100K token vocabulary
- 1 token ≈ 4 characters in English
- ₹ costs are per-token

### Step 2: Embeddings

Each token becomes a **vector** — a list of numbers representing meaning.

```
'king'  → [0.2, 0.8, 0.1, ...] (768 dimensions)
'queen' → [0.2, 0.8, 0.9, ...] (similar but different)
```

### Step 3: Attention

The model looks at ALL tokens simultaneously and decides which ones are relevant to each other.

```
'The bank by the river was steep'
'bank' attends to 'river' → means riverbank, not financial bank
```

> **Key Insight:** LLMs don't "understand" language — they predict the most likely next token based on patterns in training data. But this prediction is so good it looks like understanding.

instruction.en: See how an LLM reads text as tokens. tiktoken cannot be installed in this offline sandbox, so the starter code gives you `ToyTokenizer`, a tiny tokenizer with the same `encode(text) -> ids` and `decode(ids) -> text` methods. Complete `analyze_tokens(text, tokenizer, price_per_million=0.15)` so it returns a dict with "token_count" (number of ids), "tokens" (each id decoded on its own, as a list of strings) and "estimated_cost" (token_count * price_per_million / 1,000,000).
instruction.ta: ஒரு LLM text-ஐ tokens ஆக எப்படிப் படிக்கிறது என்று பாருங்கள். இந்த offline sandbox-ல் tiktoken-ஐ install செய்ய முடியாது, எனவே starter code-ல் அதே `encode(text) -> ids`, `decode(ids) -> text` methods கொண்ட சிறிய tokenizer ஆன `ToyTokenizer` உள்ளது. `analyze_tokens(text, tokenizer, price_per_million=0.15)`-ஐ நிறைவு செய்யுங்கள்: "token_count" (ids எண்ணிக்கை), "tokens" (ஒவ்வொரு id-ஐயும் தனியாக decode செய்த strings list), "estimated_cost" (token_count * price_per_million / 1,000,000) கொண்ட dict-ஐத் திருப்ப வேண்டும்.

practice_challenges.test_code:
_tk = ToyTokenizer()
_r = analyze_tokens("Python is the best programming language for AI development.", _tk)
assert isinstance(_r, dict), "analyze_tokens must return a dict"
assert _r.get("token_count") == 10, "the sentence has 10 tokens"
assert _r.get("tokens") == ["Python", " is", " the", " best", " programming", " language", " for", " AI", " development", "."], "tokens must be each id decoded on its own: " + repr(_r.get("tokens"))
assert abs(_r.get("estimated_cost", 0) - 10 * 0.15 / 1_000_000) < 1e-15, "estimated_cost must be token_count * 0.15 / 1,000,000"
_r2 = analyze_tokens("Rust is", _tk, price_per_million=2.0)
assert _r2["tokens"] == ["R", "u", "s", "t", " is"], "unknown words split into single characters"
assert _r2["token_count"] == 5 and abs(_r2["estimated_cost"] - 5 * 2.0 / 1_000_000) < 1e-15, "analyze_tokens must use the price_per_million argument"
assert "".join(_r2["tokens"]) == "Rust is", "joining the tokens must give back the original text"
print("All tokenizer tests passed!")

under_the_hood.summary: Inside an LLM, text is split into tokens, each token id looks up a learned vector, stacked attention layers let every position mix in information from earlier positions, and the final vector is scored against the whole vocabulary.

steps.title: Tokenization with merged pieces
steps.body: Byte-pair encoding starts from bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair seen in training text, building a vocabulary of about 100,000 pieces in GPT-4's tokenizer. Common words become one token, rare ones split: 'Hello, PyMasters!' might become ['Hello', ',', ' Py', 'Masters', '!']. In English a token averages roughly 4 characters.

steps.title: Embedding: a row lookup
steps.body: The embedding table has one row per vocabulary entry; with 100,000 tokens and 4,096 dimensions that is about 410 million numbers. Token id 15496 simply selects row 15496. These vectors are learned during training, so tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors. Position information is added so word order is not lost.

steps.title: Attention mixes context into each token
steps.body: Each token makes a query, key and value vector. A token's query is dotted with every earlier key; with scores [4, 2, 0] and key size 4, dividing by sqrt(4) gives [2, 1, 0], and softmax turns that into weights [0.67, 0.24, 0.09]. The output is the weighted sum of the value vectors: with values [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1] it is [0.76, 0.33].

props.caption: Attention for one token over three positions

steps.title: Layers stack attention and MLPs
steps.body: A transformer block applies attention and then a small feed-forward network to every position, with residual connections adding each block's result to its input. Models stack dozens of blocks; early ones tend to capture local syntax, later ones broader meaning. In a decoder model a causal mask stops any position from seeing tokens after it.

steps.title: From vector to next token
steps.body: The last position's final vector is multiplied by an output matrix to give one score per vocabulary token, softmax turns scores into probabilities, and the next token is chosen. That new token is appended and the process repeats; caches of past keys and values avoid recomputing earlier positions.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Tokens become vectors, attention lets each vector gather what it needs from the context, and many layers refine them until the last one can be scored against the vocabulary. Everything an LLM does comes from repeating that pass.
